unchanged: January 27, 2016 Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement For release at 2:00 p.m.
EST Information received since the Federal Open Market Committee met in December suggests that labor market conditions improved further even as economic growth slowed late last year.

Household spending and business fixed investment have been increasing at moderate rates in recent months, and the housing sector has improved further; however, net exports have been soft and inventory investment slowed.
A range of recent labor market indicators, including strong job gains, points to some additional decline in underutilization of labor resources.
Inflation has continued to run below the Committee's 2 percent longer-run objective, partly reflecting declines in energy prices and in prices of non-energy imports.
Market-based measures of inflation compensation declined further; survey-based measures of longer-term inflation expectations are little changed, on balance, in recent months.
Consistent with its statutory mandate, the Committee seeks to foster maximum employment and price stability.

The Committee currently expects that, with gradual adjustments in the stance of monetary policy, economic activity will expand at a moderate pace and labor market indicators will continue to strengthen.

Inflation is expected to remain low in the near term, in part because of the further declines in energy prices, but to rise to 2 percent over the medium term as the transitory effects of declines in energy and import prices dissipate and the labor market strengthens further.
The Committee is closely monitoring global economic and financial developments and is assessing their implications for the labor market and inflation, and for the balance of risks to the outlook.
Given the economic outlook, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 1/4 to 1/2 percent.
The stance of monetary policy remains accommodative, thereby supporting further improvement in labor market conditions and a return to 2 percent inflation.

In determining the timing and size of future adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will assess realized and expected economic conditions relative to its objectives of maximum employment and 2 percent inflation.

This assessment will take into account a wide range of information, including measures of labor market conditions, indicators of inflation pressures and inflation expectations, and readings on financial and international developments.
In light of the current shortfall of inflation from 2 percent, the Committee will carefully monitor actual and expected progress toward its inflation goal.

The Committee expects that economic conditions will evolve in a manner that will warrant only gradual increases in the federal funds rate; the federal funds rate is likely to remain, for some time, below levels that are expected to prevail in the longer run.
However, the actual path of the federal funds rate will depend on the economic outlook as informed by incoming data.

The Committee is maintaining its existing policy of reinvesting principal payments from its holdings of agency debt and agency mortgage-backed securities in agency mortgage-backed securities and of rolling over maturing Treasury securities at auction, and it anticipates doing so until normalization of the level of the federal funds rate is well under way.
This policy, by keeping the Committee's holdings of longer-term securities at sizable levels, should help maintain accommodative financial conditions.
Voting for the FOMC monetary policy action were: Janet L.
Yellen, Chair; William C.
Dudley, Vice Chairman; Lael Brainard; James Bullard; Stanley Fischer; Esther L.
George; Loretta J.
Mester; Jerome H.
Powell; Eric Rosengren; and Daniel K.
Tarullo.
Implementation Note issued January 27, 2016

On a 12-month basis, both inflation measures have declined this year and are running below 2 percent.
Market-based measures of inflation compensation remain low; survey-based measures of longer-term inflation expectations are little changed, on balance.
Consistent with its statutory mandate, the Committee seeks to foster maximum employment and price stability.

Hurricane-related disruptions and rebuilding will continue to affect economic activity, employment, and inflation in the near term, but past experience suggests that the storms are unlikely to materially alter the course of the national economy over the medium term.

Consequently, the Committee continues to expect that, with gradual adjustments in the stance of monetary policy, economic activity will expand at a moderate pace, and labor market conditions will strengthen somewhat further.
Inflation on a 12-month basis is expected to remain somewhat below 2 percent in the near term but to stabilize around the Committee's 2 percent objective over the medium term.
Near-term risks to the economic outlook appear roughly balanced, but the Committee is monitoring inflation developments closely.

This assessment will take into account a wide range of information, including measures of labor market conditions, indicators of inflation pressures and inflation expectations, and readings on financial and international developments.

The Committee expects that economic conditions will evolve in a manner that will warrant gradual increases in the federal funds rate; the federal funds rate is likely to remain, for some time, below levels that are expected to prevail in the longer run.

VIX has since rallied to 12.86, matching the spike level from early in the series, and the forward-looking risk premium has expanded sharply to 0.09—the highest reading in this 13-week window. This represents a regime shift I failed to anticipate.

The recent data shows volatility clustering: after stabilizing in the 11–12 range, VIX has ticked back up to 12.86 on a 4-week gain of 1.22 points. More tellingly, vol_risk_premium has compressed the gap between implied and realized volatility, now standing at 9 basis points—a 50% increase from where it started this series. The Fed's August 1 statement, while dovish in tone ("accommodative" remains the language, "roughly balanced" risks), signals a credible commitment to further gradual tightening. Market participants appear to be repricing the tail risk of policy error as the cycle extends and data remains firm.

The reversal from my previous call is material. VIX did not collapse into the 9–10s as the prior lean assumed. Instead, it has stabilized at levels that suggest a shift in underlying risk perceptions—not crash-level fear, but elevated caution. The spike in risk premium is the key tell: markets are no longer pricing implied volatility as expensive relative to recent realized moves. This is the opposite of a disinflationary easing scenario.

For the month ahead, the regime remains unstable. The evidence supports a modest rise in VIX on the basis of elevated premium and the tail risk of policy missteps in a tightening cycle, even if the Fed itself projects gradual moves.

VIX has since fallen sharply to 13.60, the lowest in this series, marking a sustained decline from 15.41 one observation ago. The vol risk premium has compressed to 0.01, the tightest on record here, indicating complacency—precisely the opposite of elevated stress that would support a "vol rising" view.

The 4-week change is now -2.75 points, continuing the downtrend. Over the last four observations, VIX has moved: 15.41 → 15.74 → 14.91 → 13.60, a steady erosion. The Fed statement (December 10) was dovish—a 25bp cut, explicit acknowledgment of elevated uncertainty and elevated downside employment risks, and messaging of willingness to adjust further—yet this dovish move was followed by or accompanied by a collapse in implied volatility, not a rise. Risk appetite has clearly reasserted itself.

The regime has shifted from the elevated volatility environment that justified my prior call. The combination of lowest-in-series VIX level, tightest vol risk premium, and sustained downward 4-week momentum points to an easing volatility regime over the next month, not a rising one.

I was wrong to hold a "vol up" view given the prior low levels and compression dynamics. The evidence now unambiguously points to further ease, at least in the near term, though the very low premium leaves little margin for surprise. A renewed shock to economic data or financial conditions could reverse this quickly.

VIX has spiked from the low 14–15 range to 31.05—a 117% increase and the highest reading in this dataset. The 4-week change shows an 11.19-point rise, the largest in the series. The vol risk premium has expanded to 0.23, double the pre-surge levels and well above any threshold suggesting mean reversion is imminent. This is not noise; it is a material widening of the volatility regime.

The FOMC language acknowledges "elevated" economic uncertainty and explicit risk to both sides of its dual mandate. Crucially, the Committee is "strongly committed" to returning inflation to 2 percent and will "adjust the stance of monetary policy as appropriate if risks emerge." A dissent by Miran for a rate cut signals fissures in consensus—inconsistent with a stable policy environment.

The gap between implied (VIX at 31) and realized volatility (inferred from the risk premium at 0.23, suggesting realized vol around 24–25) is elevated but not extreme, indicating the current level is justified by actual market turbulence rather than panic overshoot.

One month out, the onus is now on the regime to ease. The spike is recent and steep. A return to sub-20 VIX would require either a major positive surprise (Fed pivot, geopolitical de-escalation per the statement's Middle East concern) or natural mean reversion from an unsustainably high level. The language does not support imminent easing; it supports caution.

I was wrong to call this flat. The regime is now visibly in a higher state of alert.
